params.question: In triple assessment, when clinical examination suggests malignancy but the mammogram appears normal, what is the most appropriate course of action?

answers.text: Reassure the patient based on the normal imaging result

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Imaging alone cannot exclude cancer. A clinically suspicious lump with benign imaging is a discordant finding that requires further investigation, not reassurance.

Correct. When clinical and imaging findings are discordant, the suspicious component takes precedence. A normal mammogram does not rule out cancer, which is why triple assessment includes pathology as its third arm.

answers.text: Repeat mammography in six months to check for change

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Short-interval follow-up suits a BI-RADS 3 (probably benign) finding. A discordant clinical examination — where the lump feels suspicious — warrants prompt pathological investigation, not delayed reimaging.

answers.text: Request MRI to resolve the discrepancy between examination and mammogram

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI is reserved for high-risk screening (e.g. BRCA carriers) and staging of known cancer. The appropriate next step in triple assessment when findings disagree is tissue sampling, not additional imaging.

overallFeedback.feedback: When clinical examination and imaging disagree, the suspicious finding must be pursued. Imaging supports the assessment but does not replace it — that is why triple assessment combines clinical examination, imaging, and pathology.
Exactly right. Triple assessment exists because no single modality can exclude cancer on its own. When findings are discordant, the most suspicious result drives the next step.

params.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with a palpable breast lump. She has dense breast tissue. Which imaging modality should be performed first?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mammography's sensitivity drops significantly in dense breast tissue because dense tissue and cancer both appear white on X-ray. It is most reliable in older women with fattier breasts.
Correct. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging choice for women under 40 or with dense breast tissue. It uses no ionising radiation and excels at characterising focal lesions as solid or cystic.

MRI offers the highest sensitivity but is reserved for high-risk screening (e.g. BRCA mutation carriers) and staging known cancers. It generates more false positives and requires contrast injection, making it inappropriate as a first-line investigation.

answers.text: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT delivers a much higher radiation dose than mammography and is used to stage distant metastatic disease (lung, liver) in confirmed cancer. It is not used for initial assessment of a breast lump.

overallFeedback.feedback: In women under 40 or with dense breasts, ultrasound is the first-line investigation. It uses no ionising radiation and characterises focal lesions effectively, unlike mammography whose sensitivity falls in dense tissue.
Well done. Ultrasound avoids ionising radiation and performs well in dense breast tissue, making it the ideal first-line modality in younger women presenting with a lump.

params.question: A screening mammogram reveals fine, branching microcalcifications arranged in a linear pattern within one breast segment. What is the most appropriate BI-RADS category?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BI-RADS 1 indicates a completely normal mammogram. Fine, branching microcalcifications in a linear pattern are suspicious for ductal carcinoma and cannot be classified as normal.

BI-RADS 2 is reserved for definitely benign findings such as coarse, popcorn-like calcification typical of a fibroadenoma. Linear, branching microcalcifications are suspicious and require tissue sampling.

BI-RADS 3 calls for short-interval follow-up at six months. However, fine, branching microcalcifications in a linear or segmental pattern are highly suspicious for ductal carcinoma and warrant biopsy, not observation.

Correct. Fine, branching microcalcifications in a linear or segmental pattern are a hallmark mammographic finding suspicious for ductal carcinoma. BI-RADS 4 mandates tissue biopsy to confirm or exclude malignancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Fine, branching microcalcifications in a linear or segmental pattern are a classic suspicious finding for ductal carcinoma. BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) is the correct category, and it mandates tissue biopsy — each BI-RADS number carries an obligatory next step.
Excellent. Linear, branching microcalcifications are one of the most important mammographic signs of ductal carcinoma. BI-RADS 4 ensures this suspicious finding proceeds promptly to biopsy.

params.question: In a pregnant woman who discovers a breast lump, imaging assessment should be deferred until after delivery to avoid harm to the foetus.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The video emphasises that pregnancy alone never justifies skipping assessment. Ultrasound uses no ionising radiation and is safe throughout pregnancy. Every lump still requires investigation — a high-risk BI-RADS category triggers biopsy regardless of pregnancy status.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Pregnancy alone never justifies skipping breast assessment. Ultrasound is safe in pregnancy as it uses no ionising radiation, and every breast lump requires a full workup. A BI-RADS category is assigned and management follows accordingly.
